                  INTRODUCTION TO DISCOURSE ANALYSIS

A Brief Historical Overview Learning

        Discourse analysis as a whole is the work of text grammarians, working mostly with
written language. Text grammarians see texts as language elements pass into together in
relationships with one another that can be defined. Linguists have made a significant impact in
this area. Its most important contribution has been to show the links between grammar and
discourse. Discourse analysis has grown into a wide-ranging and various disciplines which find
its unity in the description of language above the sentence and an interest in the contexts and
cultural influences which affect language in use. It is also now, increasingly, forming an
environment to research in Applied Linguistics, second language learning and teaching in
particular.

        British discourse analysis was greatly influenced by M. A. K. Halliday's functional
approach to language (e.g. Halliday 1973), which in turn has connections with the Prague School
of linguists. Halliday's framework emphasizes the social functions of language and the thematic
and informational structure of speech and writing. Also important in Britain were Sinclair and
Coulthard (1975) at the University of Birmingham, who developed a model for the description of
teacher-pupil talk, based on a hierarchy of discourse units. Other similar work has dealt with
doctor patient interaction, service encounters, interviews, debates and business negotiations, as
well as monologues. Novel work in the British tradition has also been done on intonation in
discourse. The British work has principally followed structural-linguistic criteria, on the basis of
the isolation of units, and sets of rules defining well-formed sequences of discourse.

American discourse analysis has been dominated by work within the ethno methodological
tradition, which emphasizes the research method of close observation of groups of people
communicating in natural settings. It examines types of speech event such as storytelling,
greeting rituals and verbal duels in different cultural and social settings (e.g., Gumperz and
Hymes 1972). What is often called conversation analysis within the American tradition can also
be included under the general heading of discourse analysis. In conversational analysis, the
emphasis is not upon building structural models but on the close observation of the behavior of
participants in talk and on patterns which persist over a wide range of natural data. The work of
Goffman (1976; 1979), and Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson (1974) is important in the study of
conversational norms, turn taking, and other aspects of spoken interaction. Alongside the
conversation analysts, working within the sociolinguistic tradition, Labov's investigations of oral
storytelling have also contributed to a long history of interest in narrative discourse. The
American work has produced a large number of descriptions of discourse types, as well as
insights into the social constraints of politeness and face-preserving phenomena in talk,
overlapping with British work in pragmatics.

Form and Function

According McCarthy (1991), discourse analysis describes the language above the sentence: its
context and the cultural influence, which affect language in use. A discourse carries much more
than its form, it also carries its own particular function, which means that there is not necessarily
one-to-one relationship between a given supra-segmental choice and a meaning, hence form and
function might be analyzed separately in order to depict the real meaning of a discourse.
According to Halliday (1970), intonation plays a crucial role in conveying meaning. If the
intonation of a sentence is changed, its meaning will also be changed. Thus, the particular way
the sentences are produced and carry their individual meaning, and the analysis must go far
beyond sentences forms in order to be possible to depict the real meaning of the spoken
interaction.

The famous British comedy duo, Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise, started one of their shows in
1973 with the following dialogue:
Ernie: Tell me about the show.
Eric (to the audience): Have we got a show for you might folks!
Have we got a show for you! (Aside to Ernie) Have we got a
Show for them?

This short dialogue raises a number of problems for anyone wishing to do a linguistic analysis of
it; not least is the question of why it is funny (the audience laughed at Eric's question to Ernie).
Most people would agree that it is funny because Eric is playing with a grammatical structure
that seems to be ambiguous: 'Have we got a show for you!' has an inverted verb and subject.
Inversion of the verb and its subject happens only under restricted conditions in English; the
most typical circumstances in which this happens is when questions are being asked, but it also
happens in exclamations (e.g. Wasn’t my face red!). So Eric's repeated grammatical form clearly
experiences a change in how it is interpreted by the audience between its second and third
occurrence in the dialogue. Eric's inverted grammatical form in its first two occurrences clearly
has the function of an exclamation, telling the audience something, not asking them anything,
until the humorous moment when he begins to doubt whether they do have a show to offer, at

                                    POLITICAL DISCOURSE

Representation: Metaphor

One of the central concerns of political discourse is the question of how the world is presented to
the public through particular forms of linguistic representation. For example, how is language used
in attributing meaning to individuals and groups with reference to the performance of their social
practices? How are actions and events perceived and described? Which modes of reference are
used to signify places, objects and institutions within particular positive or negative frames? The
claim is that “reality” is not simply given to us through language; rather it is mediated through
different forms of language representation.

An interesting view has recently arisen in cognitive science concerning the nature of mental
representation. This view is exemplified by the following passages:
    • Most people think they can get along perfectly well without metaphor. We have found, on
       the contrary, that metaphor is persistent in everyday life, not just in language but in thought

        and action. Our ordinary conceptual system, in terms of which we both think and act, is
        fundamentally metaphorical in nature.
    •   The basic-level metaphors allow us to comprehend and draw inferences about these
        [emotion] concepts, using our knowledge of familiar, well-structured domains. In short,
        the locus of metaphor is not in language at all, but in the way we conceptualize one mental
        domain in terms of another.
    •   Human cognition is fundamentally shaped by various poetic or figurative processes.

As these quotations indicate, some researchers in cognition and language have argued that mental
representation is at least in part metaphoric. Rather than seeing metaphors as being solely or even
primarily a linguistic phenomenon, they have proposed it as a mode of representation and thought.

The reasoning behind this is that certain aspects of our knowledge are difficult for people to
represent: They are overly abstract and complex, and therefore they are represented in terms of
easier-to-understand domains, that is, metaphorically. Therefore, when we think about abstract
ideas such as inflation, the mind, or anger, we use more concrete concepts, a process which "allows
us to refer to it [an abstract concept], quantify it, identify a particular aspect of it and perhaps even
believe that we understand it" (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980).

The argument for metaphoric representation is often made as part of an argument for Cognitive
Linguistics as championed by Lakoff and his colleagues. However, I believe that the issue of
metaphoric representation is an interesting and radical idea which deserves attention in its own
right.
Lakoff (1987) and Johnson (1980) present the use of metaphor in thought as just one part of a
predominant theory of the nature of the mind. But their arguments about "objectivist metaphysics,"
generative approaches to linguistics and other controversial ideas may have drawn attention away
from this specific claim. Therefore, in this article I will examine metaphoric representation as a
theory of conceptual structure. I will not be addressing most of the other views of its proponents.
Of those views, metaphoric representation has probably had the most direct influence on
psychological research, through theories of idiom and metaphor comprehension. That said,
however, it will be impossible to avoid mentioning other views expressed by Lakoff and Johnson
(1980) or Lakoff (1987), because some of them are used to provide support for the notion of
metaphoric representation.

One disadvantage in discussing metaphoric representation is that it is necessary to discuss verbal
metaphor. And as is well known, metaphor is one of the most difficult and intransigent problems
in language. Indeed, even defining metaphor is by no means an easy task. For the present purposes,
then, a minimal description will have to serve. In verbal metaphor, there are usually two explicit
parts: a topic, which is the entity being talked about, and the vehicle, which is the metaphoric
material being predicated of the topic. (Some authors refer to these as the target and source,
respectively.) For example, in Lee is a block of ice, Lee is the topic, and block of ice is the vehicle.

linguistics anthropology
linguistics anthropology for a group of people who use the same variety of a language and who
share specific rules for speaking and for interpreting speech. It includes discourse communities
and the range and varieties of languages that members of the speech community use to interact
with each other.
Defining a speech community
there are some factors that make easier to define a speech community other than just language.
Those are social, geographical, cultural, political and ethnic factors, race, age and gender.
Discourse historical approach
Discourse analysis as a whole is the work of text grammarians, working mostly with written
language. Text grammarians see texts as language elements pass into together in relationships
with one another that can be defined. Linguists have made a significant impact in this area. Its
most important contribution has been to show the links between grammar and discourse.
Functions of according to Halliday
Michael Halliday, the founder of systemic functional linguistics, calls these three functions the
ideational, interpersonal, and textual. The ideational function is further divided into the
experiential and logical.
Endophoric referencing
 divided into anaphoric, cataphoric, and esphoric respectively refers to the previously mentioned
(preceding) information in text, information presented later in the text, the same nominal group
or phrase following the presupposed item. (Halliday and Hasan 1976). There are also personal,
demonstrative, and comparative references referring to speech situation noun pronouns like he,
him or possessive determiners like mine and yours, this, here, there, then, same, equal, so,
similarly, and otherwise
Anaphoric and cataphoric reference
In this sentence, he refers to Michael which will be treated as a anaphoric reference, and it refers
to the bank which will also be treated as an anaphoric reference. In the above given examples,
Michael and bank will be treated as cataphoric reference. Hence, an anaphoric reference occurs
when a word or phrase refers to something mentioned earlier in the discourse, whereas a
cataphoric reference occurs when a word or phrase refers to something mentioned later in the
discourse.
The social and cultural context
 of genres An important stage in genre analysis, formerly, is an examination of the social and
cultural context in which the genre is used. In the case of a written text, factors that might be
considered Include: The setting of the text
   The focus and perspective of the text

  The purpose of the text
   The intended audience for the text, their role and purpose in reading the text
The relationship between writers and readers of the text; expectations, conventions and
requirements for the text
Function Word
A distinction is often made between grammar words and lexical words in language. This
distinction also appears sometimes as function words versus content words, or empty words
versus full words.
The communicative purpose of a genre,
further, may evolve over time. It may change, it may expand or it may shrink (Swales 2004).
Communicative purpose, further, can vary across cultures even when texts belong to the same
genre category.
What is EAP?
 English for Academic Purposes (EAP) is usually defined as teaching English with the aim of
assisting learners’ study or research in that language. In this sense it is a broad term, covering all
areas of academic communicative practice such as pre-tertiary, undergraduate and post-graduate
teaching, classroom interactions, academic publishing and curriculum issues, as well as research,
student and instructional genres
systems of transitivity.
It has two components of logical and experiential functions.
In traditional grammar, transitivity was developed as the concept of transitive or intransitive
verb (Halliday, 1976) whether the verb takes an object or not, but in SFL it functions to link
grammar to the meta functions; however, in Halliday’s terms, transitivity as a major component
in experiential function of the clause deals with the “transmission of ideas “representing
‘processes’ or ‘experiences’: actions, events, processes of consciousness and relations” (1985). It
is a semantic system to analyze representations of reality in a linguistic text and create the same
experience through various lexico-grammatical options influenced by different mind styles or
authorial ideology.
Fundamental of discursive
The study of discourse and gender is an interdisciplinary endeavor undertaken by scholars in
linguistics, anthropology, communications, social psychology, education, literature, and other
disciplines.
Discursive psychology is usefully understood as working with three fundamental
observations about the nature of discourse. Discourse is:

  Oriented to action    Situated sequentially, institutionally and rhetorically
   Constructed and constructive
The three main approaches to the study of media discourse can be characterized as
  Discourse analytic
  Sociolinguistic
   Nonlinguistic
 Traditionally, rhythm has been considered an important element in the teaching of spoken
English. This is probably due to two main factors. Firstly, there does seem to be rhythmically in
varying degrees in long stretches of speech, especially carefully considered deliveries such as
broadcast talks, fluent reading aloud, speeches and monologues, as well as some ordinary
conversation. Secondly, the concept of English as a stress-timed language, deeply rooted in
theoretical and applied linguistics, has dominated approaches to the teaching of rhythm.
criteria that contribute to the development of a good and workable research topic.
In her book Qualitative Methods in Sociolinguistics, Johnstone (2000) lists a number of criteria
that contribute to the development of a good and workable research topic. In her case, she is
talking about research in the area of sociolinguistics. What she says, however, applies equally to
discourse analysis projects. These criteria include
   A well-focused idea about spoken or written discourse that is expressed as a question or a set

     SUBJECTIVE PART
       BY NIMMA MALIK
What is Transitivity?

In traditional grammar, transitivity was developed as the concept of transitive or
intransitive verb (Halliday, 1976) whether the verb takes an object or not, but in
SFL it functions to link grammar to the meta functions; however, in Halliday’s
terms, transitivity as a major component in experiential function of the clause deals
with the “transmission of ideas “representing ‘processes’ or ‘experiences’: actions,
events, processes of consciousness and relations” (1985). It is a semantic system to
analyze representations of reality in a linguistic text and create the same experience
through various lexico-grammatical options influenced by different mind styles or
authorial ideology. (Fowler, 1986).

What is Corpus? Long

A corpus is a collection of spoken or written authentic texts that is representative
of a particular area of language use, by virtue of its size and composition. It is not
always the case, however, that the corpus is representative of language use in
general, or even of a specific language variety, as the data set may be very
specialized (such as material collected from the internet) and it may not always be
based on samples of complete texts. A corpus is usually computer-readable and
able to be accessed with tools such as concordances which are able to find and sort
out language patterns. d. A general corpus, also known as a reference corpus.

A specialized corpus, as Hunston (2002) explains is:

                                                       “A corpus of texts of a
particular type, such as newspaper editorials, geography textbooks, academic
articles in a particular subject, lectures, casual conversations, essays written by
students etc. It aims to be representative of a given type of text. It is used to
investigate a particular type of language.”

Specialized corpora are required when the research question relates to the use of
spoken or written discourse in particular kinds of texts or in particular situations. A
specialized corpus might be used, for example, to examine the use of hedges in
casual conversation or the ways in which people signal a change in topic in an
academic presentation.

Five needed terms before deciding a topic.

A research topic is your general area of interest, whereas the research question is
the particular thing you want to find out and which grows out of your research
topic (Sunderland 2010). When deciding on a topic, there are a few things that you
will need to do:

      brainstorm for ideas
      choose a topic that will enable you to read and understand the literature
      ensure that the topic is manageable and that material is available
      make a list of key words
      be flexible
      define your topic as a focused research question
      research and read more about your topic
      formulate a thesis statement

What are the factors of Multimedia discourse analysis?

Multimedia discourse analysis is a field that examines how meaning is constructed
and communicated through multimedia, which includes a combination of text,
images, sound, and video.

Factors:

    Discourse analytic
    Sociolinguistic

    Nonlinguistic

Johnstone research project explain.

In her book Qualitative Methods in Sociolinguistics, Johnstone (2000) lists a
number of criteria that contribute to the development of a good and workable
research topic. In her case, she is talking about research in the area of
sociolinguistics. What she says, however, applies equally to discourse analysis
projects. These criteria include:

    Ability to get the discourse data that is needed for the research project.
    A well-focused idea about spoken or written discourse that is expressed as a
     question or a set of closely related questions;
    An understanding of how discourse analytic techniques can be used to
     answer the research question you are asking;
    An understanding of why your question about spoken or written discourse
     are important in a wider context; that is, why answering the question will
     have practical value and/or be of interest to the world at large;
    Familiarity with and access to the location where your discourse analysis
     project will be carried out;
    The time it will realistically take to carry out the discourse analysis project,
     analyze the results and write up the results of the project;
    Being comfortable with and competent in the ways of collecting the
     discourse data required by the project;
    Being competent in the method of analysis required for the project.

What are kinds of discourse analysis?

   1) Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)
   2) Conversation Analysis (CA)
   3) Narrative Analysis
   4) Multimodal Discourse Analysis
   5) Discursive Psychology
   6) Pragmatics and Speech Act Theory
   7) Corpus-Based Discourse Analysis
   8) Genre Analysis
   9) Political Discourse Analysis

   10)       Historical Discourse Analysis
   11)       Cognitive Linguistic Discourse Analysis
   12)       Intercultural Discourse Analysis

Question: What is one of the central concerns of political discourse
analysis?
Answer: The central concern is how language represents the world to the
public through various linguistic forms.

Question: How is language used in attributing meaning to individuals
and groups in political discourse?
Answer: Language is used to attribute meaning to individuals and groups
by describing their social practices and actions.

Question: According to cognitive science, what is the nature of
mental representation?
Answer: Cognitive science suggests that mental representation is, at least
in part, metaphoric in nature.

Question: How do people use metaphor in everyday life, according to
cognitive science?
Answer: Metaphor is persistent in everyday life and is used not just in
language but in thought and action.

Question: What role do basic-level metaphors play in comprehension,
as suggested by cognitive science?
Answer: Basic-level metaphors allow us to comprehend and draw
inferences about concepts using our knowledge of familiar domains.

Question: How does cognitive linguistics view metaphors?
Answer: Cognitive linguistics sees metaphors as a mode of representation
and thought, not solely a linguistic phenomenon.

Question: Why do we use metaphors when thinking about abstract
ideas, as per Lakoff and Johnson?

Answer: We use metaphors to represent abstract ideas because they are
difficult to represent directly and are better understood through concrete
concepts.

Question: What are some arguments presented in favor of metaphoric
representation?
Answer: Metaphoric representation helps us refer to abstract concepts,
quantify them, and identify specific aspects, making them more
understandable.

Question: Why is the issue of metaphoric representation considered
interesting and radical?
Answer: The issue of metaphoric representation is interesting and radical
because it challenges traditional views of how language and thought are
interconnected.

Question: How has metaphoric representation influenced
psychological research?
Answer: Metaphoric representation has influenced psychological research,
particularly in theories of idiom and metaphor comprehension.

Question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of discussing
metaphoric representation?
Answer: The advantage is gaining insights into how abstract ideas are
represented, but the disadvantage is the challenge of defining and
discussing verbal metaphors.

Question: How did critical linguistics emerge in the late 1970s?

Answer: Critical linguistics emerged from Halliday's functional linguistic
theory, viewing language as a "social fact" displaying politics and ideology
through grammatical structure.

Question: What is Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) and how is it
related to critical linguistics?
Answer: CDA is a broader analytic program analyzing language to uncover
power abuse and inequality in society, and it relates to critical linguistics as
a part of this program.

Question: How does Van Dijk define CDA, and what is the aim of this
approach?
Answer: Van Dijk defines CDA as a form of critically driven theory and
practice aiming to study power abuse and inequality using various
methods.

Question: What are some criticisms of the critical approach in CDA?
Answer: The approach has been criticized for potentially confirming
preconceived notions and for using linguistic analysis to support claims of
power abuse.

Question: Who are some influential scholars in the field of political
discourse and CDA?
Answer: Scholars like Norman Fairclough, Ruth Wodak, and Teun van Dijk
have been leaders in both political discourse and CDA.

Question: How does the critical analyst view political discourse?
Answer: The critical analyst views political discourse as the use of
language and discursive positioning to hide or distribute responsibility and
designate specific individuals or groups for political purposes.

Question: What is the relationship between political discourse and
phonetics/phonology?
Answer: There has been relatively little attention given to how politicians
use phonetic and phonological features of language for political purposes.

Question: How does Margaret Thatcher's speech modification
illustrate the impact of phonetics in political persuasion?
Answer: Margaret Thatcher modified her speech to appeal to voters and
enhance her political image.

Question: How does the study of prosody in political interviews reveal
politicians' communication style?
Answer: Politicians tend to reflect a positive and fluid communication style
in political interviews.
Question: How have prosodic features been harnessed in political
debates to achieve specific effects?
Answer: In political debates, politicians use prosodic features such as pitch,
emphasis, and focus to convey assertiveness, irony, emotion, and
hyperbole to achieve specific political goals.

Question: How does advertising exemplify the diverse roles of
discourse in society?
Answer: Advertising serves as a form of discourse that informs, influences,
and relates to different social spheres and activities.

Question: Why does advertising sometimes have a perceived
marginal status in discourse analysis?
Answer: Advertising's ability to draw inspiration from various sources and
its ultimate commercial aims contribute to its perceived marginality.

Question: What are the primary aims of advertising messages?

Q. Define media discourse?
Media discourse refers to interactions that take place through a broadcast platform,
whether spoken or written, in which the discourse is oriented to a non-present reader,
listener or viewer. Though the discourse is oriented towards these recipients, they
very often cannot make instantaneous responses to the producer of the discourse,
though increasingly this is changing with the advent of new media technology, as
we shall explore. Crucially, the written or spoken discourse itself is oriented to the
readership or listening/viewing audience, respectively. In other words, media
discourse is a public, manufactured, on-record, form of interaction. It is not ad hoc
or spontaneous (in the same way as casual speaking or writing is); it is neither private
nor off the record. Obvious as these basic characteristics may sound, they are crucial
to the investigation, description and understanding of media discourse.
Q. Confidentiality
It refers to a condition in which the researcher knows the identity of a research
subject, but takes steps to protect that identity from being discovered by others. Most
human subject’s research requires collection of a sign consent agreement from
participants, and thus researchers are aware of the identity of their subjects. In such
cases, maintaining confidentiality is a key measure to ensure the protection of private
information.
Q. Sociolinguistics
The term “sociolinguistic” for work that involves variation and style in the media or
a similar close analysis of language. Sociolinguistic insights, either to characterize
some dimension of media language, such as variation and style, or to inform related
discourse level work, such as genre and register. The “nonlinguistic” research
involves work in political science, media studies, or communication studies
paradigms and, to some degree, in cultural studies. Nonlinguistic domains are
referred to by media discourse researchers perhaps more than in any other topical
area of discourse analysis.

Q. How have modern communication platforms, such as social media or texting, influenced
the use and evolution of discourse markers?

SOLUTION:
In today's digital age, communication platforms like social media and texting have significantly
impacted the use and development of discourse markers—those small words or phrases that
structure conversations. Emoji’s and Stickers employed to convey emotions and tone in brief
digital exchanges, addressing the challenges of expressing sarcasm, humor, or excitement
through text alone.
Abbreviations and acronyms like LOL, OMG, or BRB have become commonplace discourse
markers in digital communication, helping convey reactions, express agreement, or signal
pauses. These shortcuts have integrated into online language, contributing to the evolution of
discourse markers.
Social media platforms have introduced new methods of signaling discourse through features
like hashtags, mentions, and emojis. Hashtags categorize and connect posts on similar topics,
mentions direct messages to specific individuals, fostering interaction. Emojis provide visual
cues, enhancing the conveyance of emotions and reactions in texts.
In essence, modern communication platforms have shaped the adaptation and evolution of
discourse markers by aligning with the rapid, brief nature of digital communication. These
platforms offer tools that enable effective self-expression, meaning conveyance, and interaction
in the digital era.

Q. How do discourse markers contribute to the structure and coherence of conversations?

SOLUTION:
Discourse markers are essential for structuring and enhancing the coherence of conversations.
They signal relationships between different parts of a conversation, guiding the audience through
the flow of information. Here's a summary of their contributions:
Signaling Relationships:
Addition: Markers like "and," "also," and "moreover" connect related ideas, contributing to a
logical flow.
Contrast: Words such as "but" and "however" highlight differences or contrasts between ideas.
Causation: Markers like "because" and "therefore" indicate cause-and-effect relationships.
Enumeration: Words like "firstly" and "secondly" organize information, aiding audience
comprehension.
Managing Turn-Taking:
Discourse markers like "well" and "so" signal transitions between speakers or topics, enhancing
overall coherence.
Expressing Attitude and Politeness:
Markers like "please" and "thank you" contribute to the politeness and tone of a conversation,
shaping its cohesion.
Providing Clarification:
Words such as "in other words" and "for example" clarify and elaborate on statements, ensuring
audience understanding.
Highlighting Important Information:
Certain markers like "indeed" and "in fact" emphasize key points, drawing attention to critical
information.
Expressing Uncertainty or Hedging:
Markers like "perhaps" and "maybe" convey uncertainty, adding nuance to the conversation.
In essence, discourse markers act as linguistic signposts, guiding the audience through
conversation structure, expressing relationships between ideas, managing transitions, and
contributing to overall coherence and understanding.

ENG523_Glossary

 1. Adjacency pairs: An adjacency pair is a unit of conversation that
   contains an exchange of one turn each by two speakers. The turns
   are functionally related to each other in such a fashion that the first
   turn requires a certain type or range of types of second turn.
 2. Big “C” Conversations (Tools of Inquiry): “Conversations” (with
   a capital “C”) are debates in society or within specific social groups
   (over focused issues like smoking, abortion, or school reform) that
   large numbers of people recognize, both in terms of what “sides”
   there are to take in such debates and what sorts of people tend to be
   on each side.
 3. Collocational Patterns: Any pattern of words or grammatical
   structures (types of words and phrases and clauses) that “hang
   together” to betoken a particular social language (and the identity
   associated with it) in the way in which sun hat, swimsuit, sunscreen,
   a towel, and flip-flops “hang together” to betoken a “sunbather.”
 4. Conversational Analysis: A detailed form of discourse analysis
   that sees conversation as the basic human communicational form
   and seeks to explicate how people produce and reproduce social
   order through talk and orientation to talk and each other in social
   interaction. The approach is almost always just spelled as “CA” and
   is a branch of sociology (one that gives up building grand
   sociological theories in favor of describing the order people actually

By ASFAND YARR

                         ENG523_Glossary

   create and how they create and sustain that order). Manny Schegloff
   at the University of California at Los Angeles is the best living
   practitioner of CA.
 5. Critical Discourse Analysis: Any form of discourse analysis that
   seeks to engage with politics (see the Glossary entry for “politics”).
   Critical discourse analysis deals with whose “interests” are
   represented, helped, or harmed as people speak and write. When
   “critical discourse analysis” is spelled as “CDA” it often refers to
   the work of Norman Fairclough and his associates.
 6. Eliciting Exchange: The most common exchange in the classroom
   is an eliciting exchange (Willis, 1992, pg.113). These exchanges
   begin with the teacher asking a question (usually one they already
   know the answer to).
 7. Identity: A word used for lots of different things. What I mean by
   it in this book is this: Different ways of being in the world at
   different times and places for different purposes; for example, ways
   of being a “good student,” an “avid bird watcher,” a “mainstream

ENG523_Glossary

 1. Adjacency pairs: An adjacency pair is a unit of conversation that
   contains an exchange of one turn each by two speakers. The turns
   are functionally related to each other in such a fashion that the first
   turn requires a certain type or range of types of second turn.
 2. Big “C” Conversations (Tools of Inquiry): “Conversations” (with
   a capital “C”) are debates in society or within specific social groups
   (over focused issues like smoking, abortion, or school reform) that
   large numbers of people recognize, both in terms of what “sides”
   there are to take in such debates and what sorts of people tend to be
   on each side.
 3. Collocational Patterns: Any pattern of words or grammatical
   structures (types of words and phrases and clauses) that “hang
   together” to betoken a particular social language (and the identity
   associated with it) in the way in which sun hat, swimsuit, sunscreen,
   a towel, and flip-flops “hang together” to betoken a “sunbather.”
 4. Conversational Analysis: A detailed form of discourse analysis
   that sees conversation as the basic human communicational form
   and seeks to explicate how people produce and reproduce social
   order through talk and orientation to talk and each other in social
   interaction. The approach is almost always just spelled as “CA” and
   is a branch of sociology (one that gives up building grand
   sociological theories in favor of describing the order people actually

By ASFAND YARR

                         ENG523_Glossary

   create and how they create and sustain that order). Manny Schegloff
   at the University of California at Los Angeles is the best living
   practitioner of CA.
 5. Critical Discourse Analysis: Any form of discourse analysis that
   seeks to engage with politics (see the Glossary entry for “politics”).
   Critical discourse analysis deals with whose “interests” are
   represented, helped, or harmed as people speak and write. When
   “critical discourse analysis” is spelled as “CDA” it often refers to

   is an eliciting exchange (Willis, 1992, pg.113). These exchanges
   begin with the teacher asking a question (usually one they already

Discourse Analysis (ENG523)                                                                     VU

                  INTRODUCTION TO DISCOURSE ANALYSIS

A Brief Historical Overview Learning

        Discourse analysis as a whole is the work of text grammarians, working mostly with
written language. Text grammarians see texts as language elements pass into together in
relationships with one another that can be defined. Linguists have made a significant impact in
this area. Its most important contribution has been to show the links between grammar and
discourse. Discourse analysis has grown into a wide-ranging and various disciplines which find
its unity in the description of language above the sentence and an interest in the contexts and
cultural influences which affect language in use. It is also now, increasingly, forming an
environment to research in Applied Linguistics, second language learning and teaching in
particular.

        British discourse analysis was greatly influenced by M. A. K. Halliday's functional
approach to language (e.g. Halliday 1973), which in turn has connections with the Prague School
of linguists. Halliday's framework emphasizes the social functions of language and the thematic
and informational structure of speech and writing. Also important in Britain were Sinclair and
Coulthard (1975) at the University of Birmingham, who developed a model for the description of
teacher-pupil talk, based on a hierarchy of discourse units. Other similar work has dealt with
doctor patient interaction, service encounters, interviews, debates and business negotiations, as
well as monologues. Novel work in the British tradition has also been done on intonation in
discourse. The British work has principally followed structural-linguistic criteria, on the basis of
the isolation of units, and sets of rules defining well-formed sequences of discourse.

American discourse analysis has been dominated by work within the ethno methodological
tradition, which emphasizes the research method of close observation of groups of people
communicating in natural settings. It examines types of speech event such as storytelling,
greeting rituals and verbal duels in different cultural and social settings (e.g., Gumperz and
Hymes 1972). What is often called conversation analysis within the American tradition can also
be included under the general heading of discourse analysis. In conversational analysis, the
emphasis is not upon building structural models but on the close observation of the behavior of
participants in talk and on patterns which persist over a wide range of natural data. The work of
Goffman (1976; 1979), and Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson (1974) is important in the study of
conversational norms, turn taking, and other aspects of spoken interaction. Alongside the
conversation analysts, working within the sociolinguistic tradition, Labov's investigations of oral
storytelling have also contributed to a long history of interest in narrative discourse. The
American work has produced a large number of descriptions of discourse types, as well as
insights into the social constraints of politeness and face-preserving phenomena in talk,
overlapping with British work in pragmatics.

                              ©Copyright Virtual University of Pakistan                           2

Discourse Analysis (ENG523)                                                                      VU

Form and Function

According McCarthy (1991), discourse analysis describes the language above the sentence: its
context and the cultural influence, which affect language in use. A discourse carries much more
than its form, it also carries its own particular function, which means that there is not necessarily
one-to-one relationship between a given supra-segmental choice and a meaning, hence form and
function might be analyzed separately in order to depict the real meaning of a discourse.
According to Halliday (1970), intonation plays a crucial role in conveying meaning. If the
intonation of a sentence is changed, its meaning will also be changed. Thus, the particular way
the sentences are produced and carry their individual meaning, and the analysis must go far
beyond sentences forms in order to be possible to depict the real meaning of the spoken
interaction.

The famous British comedy duo, Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise, started one of their shows in
1973 with the following dialogue:
Ernie: Tell me about the show.
Eric (to the audience): Have we got a show for you might folks!
Have we got a show for you! (Aside to Ernie) Have we got a
Show for them?

This short dialogue raises a number of problems for anyone wishing to do a linguistic analysis of
it; not least is the question of why it is funny (the audience laughed at Eric's question to Ernie).
Most people would agree that it is funny because Eric is playing with a grammatical structure
that seems to be ambiguous: 'Have we got a show for you!' has an inverted verb and subject.
Inversion of the verb and its subject happens only under restricted conditions in English; the
most typical circumstances in which this happens is when questions are being asked, but it also
happens in exclamations (e.g. Wasn’t my face red!). So Eric's repeated grammatical form clearly
experiences a change in how it is interpreted by the audience between its second and third
occurrence in the dialogue. Eric's inverted grammatical form in its first two occurrences clearly
has the function of an exclamation, telling the audience something, not asking them anything,
until the humorous moment when he begins to doubt whether they do have a show to offer, at
which point he uses the same grammatical form to ask Ernie a genuine question. There seems,
then, to be a lack of one-to-one correspondence between grammatical form and communicative
function; the inverted form in itself does not inherently carry an exclamatory or a questioning

                                  POLITICAL DISCOURSE

Representation: Metaphor

One of the central concerns of political discourse is the question of how the world is presented to
the public through particular forms of linguistic representation. For example, how is language
used in attributing meaning to individuals and groups with reference to the performance of their
social practices? How are actions and events perceived and described? Which modes of
reference are used to signify places, objects and institutions within particular positive or negative
frames? The claim is that “reality” is not simply given to us through language; rather it is
mediated through different forms of language representation.

An interesting view has recently arisen in cognitive science concerning the nature of mental
representation. This view is exemplified by the following passages:
     Most people think they can get along perfectly well without metaphor. We have found,
       on the contrary, that metaphor is persistent in everyday life, not just in language but in
       thought and action. Our ordinary conceptual system, in terms of which we both think and
       act, is fundamentally metaphorical in nature.
     The basic-level metaphors allow us to comprehend and draw inferences about these
       [emotion] concepts, using our knowledge of familiar, well-structured domains. In short,
       the locus of metaphor is not in language at all, but in the way we conceptualize one
       mental domain in terms of another.
     Human cognition is fundamentally shaped by various poetic or figurative processes.

As these quotations indicate, some researchers in cognition and language have argued that
mental representation is at least in part metaphoric. Rather than seeing metaphors as being solely

Form and Function

According McCarthy (1991), discourse analysis describes the language above the sentence: its
context and the cultural influence, which affect language in use. A discourse carries much more
than its form, it also carries its own particular function, which means that there is not necessarily
one-to-one relationship between a given supra-segmental choice and a meaning, hence form and
function might be analyzed separately in order to depict the real meaning of a discourse.
According to Halliday (1970), intonation plays a crucial role in conveying meaning. If the
intonation of a sentence is changed, its meaning will also be changed. Thus, the particular way
the sentences are produced and carry their individual meaning, and the analysis must go far
beyond sentences forms in order to be possible to depict the real meaning of the spoken
interaction.

The famous British comedy duo, Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise, started one of their shows in
1973 with the following dialogue:
Ernie: Tell me about the show.
Eric (to the audience): Have we got a show for you might folks!
Have we got a show for you! (Aside to Ernie) Have we got a
Show for them?

This short dialogue raises a number of problems for anyone wishing to do a linguistic analysis of
it; not least is the question of why it is funny (the audience laughed at Eric's question to Ernie).
Most people would agree that it is funny because Eric is playing with a grammatical structure
that seems to be ambiguous: 'Have we got a show for you!' has an inverted verb and subject.
Inversion of the verb and its subject happens only under restricted conditions in English; the
most typical circumstances in which this happens is when questions are being asked, but it also
happens in exclamations (e.g. Wasn’t my face red!). So Eric's repeated grammatical form clearly
experiences a change in how it is interpreted by the audience between its second and third
occurrence in the dialogue. Eric's inverted grammatical form in its first two occurrences clearly
has the function of an exclamation, telling the audience something, not asking them anything,
until the humorous moment when he begins to doubt whether they do have a show to offer, at
which point he uses the same grammatical form to ask Ernie a genuine question. There seems,
then, to be a lack of one-to-one correspondence between grammatical form and communicative
function; the inverted form in itself does not inherently carry an exclamatory or a questioning

participants in talk and on patterns which persist over a wide range of natural data. The work of
Goffman (1976; 1979), and Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson (1974) is important in the study of
conversational norms, turn taking, and other aspects of spoken interaction. Alongside the
conversation analysts, working within the sociolinguistic tradition, Labov's investigations of oral
storytelling have also contributed to a long history of interest in narrative discourse. The
American work has produced a large number of descriptions of discourse types, as well as
insights into the social constraints of politeness and face-preserving phenomena in talk,
overlapping with British work in pragmatics.

Form and Function

According McCarthy (1991), discourse analysis describes the language above the sentence: its
context and the cultural influence, which affect language in use. A discourse carries much more
than its form, it also carries its own particular function, which means that there is not necessarily
one-to-one relationship between a given supra-segmental choice and a meaning, hence form and
function might be analyzed separately in order to depict the real meaning of a discourse.
According to Halliday (1970), intonation plays a crucial role in conveying meaning. If the
intonation of a sentence is changed, its meaning will also be changed. Thus, the particular way
the sentences are produced and carry their individual meaning, and the analysis must go far
beyond sentences forms in order to be possible to depict the real meaning of the spoken
interaction.

The famous British comedy duo, Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise, started one of their shows in
1973 with the following dialogue:
Ernie: Tell me about the show.
Eric (to the audience): Have we got a show for you might folks!
Have we got a show for you! (Aside to Ernie) Have we got a
Show for them?

This short dialogue raises a number of problems for anyone wishing to do a linguistic analysis of
it; not least is the question of why it is funny (the audience laughed at Eric's question to Ernie).
Most people would agree that it is funny because Eric is playing with a grammatical structure
that seems to be ambiguous: 'Have we got a show for you!' has an inverted verb and subject.
Inversion of the verb and its subject happens only under restricted conditions in English; the
most typical circumstances in which this happens is when questions are being asked, but it also
happens in exclamations (e.g. Wasn’t my face red!). So Eric's repeated grammatical form clearly
experiences a change in how it is interpreted by the audience between its second and third
occurrence in the dialogue. Eric's inverted grammatical form in its first two occurrences clearly
has the function of an exclamation, telling the audience something, not asking them anything,
until the humorous moment when he begins to doubt whether they do have a show to offer, at
which point he uses the same grammatical form to ask Ernie a genuine question. There seems,
then, to be a lack of one-to-one correspondence between grammatical form and communicative
function; the inverted form in itself does not inherently carry an exclamatory or a questioning

ENG523
1. Discourse Analysis

The study of language use beyond the sentence level, focusing on how meaning is constructed in
different contexts and social interactions.

2. Text Grammarians

Experts who analyze written texts to understand relationships between linguistic elements,
focusing on how these elements form coherent structures.

3. Functional Linguistics

An approach that examines language based on its social functions, emphasizing how grammar
interacts with meaning and context.

4. Halliday’s Framework

A model by M.A.K. Halliday that views language as a system of choices influenced by social
functions, focusing on thematic and informational structures.

5. Context and Culture in Language

The idea that language use is shaped by its context and cultural influences, affecting how it is
interpreted and used.

6. Pragmatics

A branch of linguistics that studies how context influences the interpretation of meaning,
including speaker intentions and implied meanings.

7. Speech Acts

Actions performed via language, such as requesting, apologizing, or commanding. Speech acts
analyze what the speaker intends to accomplish.

8. Intonation in Discourse

The rise and fall of pitch in speech, which can change the meaning of a statement and reflect
emotions or emphasis.

9. Cohesion

The linguistic connections within a text that link sentences together, such as pronouns,
conjunctions, or lexical repetition.

10. Coherence

The logical and meaningful connection of ideas in a text, ensuring it "makes sense" to the reader
or listener.

11. Turn-Taking

The structured process of managing conversational turns, ensuring participants know when to
speak or listen.

12. Adjacency Pairs

Paired utterances in conversation where the first part predicts a specific type of response, like a
question-answer or greeting-reply sequence.

13. Initiating Moves

The first action in an interaction, such as asking a question or making a statement, to start a
conversational exchange.

14. Eliciting Exchanges

Interactions where one speaker seeks specific information, often seen in classroom settings, such
as teacher questions and student responses.

15. Boundary Exchanges

Discourse structures that signal transitions or divisions within conversations, such as shifting
topics or concluding segments.

16. Transactional Language

Language used to achieve specific tasks or exchange information, such as ordering food or
asking for directions.

17. Interactional Talk

Language used for social purposes, like building relationships or maintaining communication, as
in casual conversations.

18. Discourse Markers

Words or phrases, such as well, so, or you know, used to organize speech, manage turn-taking, or
signal shifts in topic.

19. Genre vs. Text Type

Genres are culturally recognized categories like novels or essays, while text types (e.g., narrative,
descriptive) focus on structural properties of texts.

20. Problem-Solution Pattern

A common discourse structure presenting a situation, identifying a problem, proposing a
solution, and evaluating the result.

21. Claim-Counterclaim Pattern

A structure where a claim is stated and challenged by a counterclaim, often used in debates and
argumentative texts.

22. General-Specific Pattern

A pattern where a general idea is followed by specific examples or details, commonly found in
academic writing.

23. Cultural Rhetoric

The study of how cultural beliefs and values shape rhetorical practices and language use in
different societies.

24. Comparative Rhetoric

A cross-cultural analysis of rhetorical traditions, highlighting differences and similarities in
communication styles.

25. Schema Theory

A theory stating that readers use their prior knowledge (schemata) to interpret and understand
texts.

26. Illocutionary Acts

The intended function of a speech act, such as asserting, questioning, or commanding.

27. Speech Events

Specific communicative situations, like interviews, lectures, or debates, each with its own norms
and conventions.

28. Discourse Units

Segments of language that form coherent sections of discourse, such as paragraphs, turns, or
entire conversations.

29. Conversational Analysis

A method of studying the structure and patterns of spoken interaction, focusing on turn-taking
and conversational norms.

30. Politeness Theory

A framework analyzing how speakers maintain social harmony by managing face (self-image)
through politeness strategies.

31. Face-Saving Strategies

Techniques used to avoid threatening someone's self-image in conversation, such as softening
criticism.

32. Back-Channeling

Listeners' verbal or non-verbal cues (e.g., mm-hmm, nodding) to show attention and encourage
the speaker.

33. Transactional Model

A communication model where participants exchange messages simultaneously, influencing
each other interactively.

34. Overlapping Talk

When two or more speakers talk at the same time, often signaling enthusiasm or competition for
the floor.

35. Topic Management

The skill of maintaining, shifting, or closing topics in conversation.

36. Foregrounded Information

Highlighted or emphasized information in discourse that the speaker wants to focus on.

37. Backgrounded Information

Information given less emphasis or treated as secondary in a discourse.

38. Intercultural Communication

Communication between individuals from different cultural backgrounds, requiring sensitivity to
cultural norms and values.

39. Narrative Discourse

The structure and function of storytelling, focusing on how events and characters are presented.

40. Textual Patterns

Recognizable structures within texts, like cause-effect or compare-contrast, aiding
comprehension and organization.

41. Explicitness in Written Text

The degree to which a text clearly conveys meaning without relying on shared context or
assumptions.

42. Reader-Text Interaction

How readers engage with and interpret a text, influenced by their background knowledge and
expectations.

43. Critical Discourse Analysis

A method of examining how power and ideology are reflected and constructed in language use.

      Critical Discourse: An interdisciplinary approach to the study of language
      and communication that focuses on how language reproduces social
      inequalities, power relations, and ideologies.
      Coherent discourse: A text or communication that is logically connected,
      consistent, and easy to follow, with a clear meaning or message.
      Situational Context: The environment, circumstances, and social setting in
      which communication takes place, influencing the meaning and interpretation
      of language.
      Reference discourse: A term used in CDA to describe the dominant or
      standard language variety used in a particular context or community, often
      associated with power and prestige.
      Conversation Analysis: A methodology for studying social interactions,
      particularly conversations, to understand how people use language to create
      social order and meaning.
      Discourse community: A group of people who share a common language,
      values, and practices, often with a shared goal or interest, and who use
      language to construct and maintain their identity and relationships.
      Race/racism: Social constructs used to categorize people into groups based
      on physical characteristics, often leading to discrimination, prejudice, and
      inequality.
      spoken discourse: Language use in face-to-face interactions, such as
      conversations, meetings, and discussions.
      Prejudice: A preconceived negative judgment or attitude towards a person or
      group, often based on stereotypes or biases.
      Expressive: A type of language function that expresses the speaker's feelings,
      emotions, or attitudes.
      Informative: A type of language function that conveys information,
      knowledge, or facts.
      Declarative: A type of sentence that states a fact or opinion, often used to
      make assertions or declarations.
      Narrative Discourse: A type of language use that tells a story or recounts an
      event or experience.
      Discourse analysis: A broad field of study that examines language use in
      social contexts to understand how language creates meaning and constructs
      social relationships.

written language. Text grammarians see texts as language elements pass into together
in relationships with one another that can be defined. Linguists have made a significant
impact in this area. Its most important contribution has been to show the links between
grammar and discourse.

Functions of according to Halliday

Michael Halliday, the founder of systemic functional linguistics, calls these three
functions the ideational, interpersonal, and textual. The ideational function is further
divided into the experiential and logical.

Endophoric referencing

divided into anaphoric, cataphoric, and esphoric respectively refers to the previously
mentioned (preceding) information in text, information presented later in the text, the
same nominal group or phrase following the presupposed item. (Halliday and Hasan
1976). There are also personal, demonstrative, and comparative references referring to
speech situation noun pronouns like he, him or possessive determiners like mine and
yours, this, here, there, then, same, equal, so, similarly, and otherwise

Anaphoric and cataphoric reference

In this sentence, he refers to Michael which will be treated as an anaphoric reference,
and it refers to the bank which will also be treated as an anaphoric reference. In the
above given examples, Michael and bank will be treated as cataphoric reference. Hence,
an anaphoric reference occurs when a word or phrase refers to something mentioned
earlier in the discourse, whereas a cataphoric reference occurs when a word or phrase
refers to something mentioned later in the discourse.

The social and cultural context

of genres an important stage in genre analysis, formerly, is an examination of the social
and cultural context in which the genre is used. In the case of a written text, factors that
might be considered Include:

      The setting of the text
      The focus and perspective of the text.
      The purpose of the text
      The intended audience for the text, their role and purpose in reading the text
      The relationship between writers and readers of the text; expectations,
       conventions and requirements for the text

Function Word

A distinction is often made between grammar words and lexical words in language.
This distinction also appears sometimes as function words versus content words, or
empty words versus full words.

The communicative purpose of a genre,

further, may evolve over time. It may change, it may expand or it may shrink (Swales
2004). Communicative purpose, further, can vary across cultures even when texts
belong to the same genre category.

What is EAP?

English for Academic Purposes (EAP) is usually defined as teaching English with the aim
of assisting learners' study or research in that language. In this sense it is a broad term,
covering all areas of academic communicative practice such as pre-tertiary,
undergraduate and postgraduate teaching, classroom interactions, academic
publishing, and curriculum issues, as well as research, student and instructional genres

systems of transitivity.

It has two components of logical and experiential functions.

In traditional grammar, transitivity was developed as the concept of transitive or
intransitive verb (Halliday, 1976) whether the verb takes an object or not, but in SFL it
functions to link grammar to the meta functions; however, in Halliday's terms, transitivity
as a major component in experiential function of the clause deals with the "transmission
of ideas “representing 'processes' or 'experiences': actions, events, processes of
consciousness and relations" (1985). It is a semantic system to analyze representations
of reality in a linguistic text and create the same experience through various lexico-
grammatical options influenced by different mind styles or authorial ideology.

Fundamental of discursive

The study of discourse and gender is an interdisciplinary endeavor undertaken by
scholars in linguistics, anthropology, communications, social psychology, education,
literature, and other disciplines.

Discursive psychology is usefully understood as working with three fundamental

observations about the nature of discourse. Discourse is:

Oriented to action Situated sequentially, institutionally and rhetorically

Constructed and constructive

The three main approaches to the study of media discourse can be characterized as

Discourse analytic

Sociolinguistic

Nonlinguistic

Traditionally, rhythm has been considered an important element in the teaching of
spoken English.

This is probably due to two main factors. Firstly, there does seem to be rhythmically in
varying degrees in long stretches of speech, especially carefully considered deliveries
such as broadcast talks, fluent reading aloud, speeches and monologues, as well as
some ordinary conversation. Secondly, the concept of English as a stress-timed
language, deeply rooted in theoretical and applied linguistics, has dominated
approaches to the teaching of rhythm.

Discourse historical approach

Discourse analysis as a whole is the work of text grammarians, working mostly with written language. Text grammarians see
texts as language elements pass into together in relationships with one another that can be defined. Linguists have made a
significant impact in this area. Its most important contribution has been to show the links between grammar and discourse.

Functions of according to Halliday

Michael Halliday, the founder of systemic functional linguistics, calls these three functions the ideational, interpersonal, and
textual. The ideational function is further divided into the experiential and logical.

Endophoric referencing divided into anaphoric, cataphoric, and esphoric respectively refers to the previously mentioned
(preceding) information in text, information presented later in the text, the same nominal group or phrase following the
presupposed item. (Halliday and Hasan 1976). There are also personal, demonstrative, and comparative references referring
to speech situation noun pronouns like he, him or possessive determiners like mine and yours, this, here, there, then, same,
equal, so, similarly, and otherwise

Anaphoric and cataphoric reference

In this sentence, he refers to Michael which will be treated as an anaphoric reference, and it refers to the bank which will
also be treated as an anaphoric reference. In the above given examples, Michael and bank will be treated as cataphoric
reference. Hence, an anaphoric reference occurs when a word or phrase refers to something mentioned earlier in the
discourse, whereas a cataphoric reference occurs when a word or phrase refers to something mentioned later in the
discourse.

 The social and cultural context of genres an important stage in genre analysis, formerly, is an examination of the social and
cultural context in which the genre is used. In the case of a written text, factors that might be considered Include:

    •   The setting of the text
    •   The focus and perspective of the text.
    •   The purpose of the text
    •   The intended audience for the text, their role and purpose in reading the text
    •   The relationship between writers and readers of the text; expectations, conventions and requirements for the text

Function Word

A distinction is often made between grammar words and lexical words in language. This distinction also appears sometimes
as function words versus content words, or empty words versus full words.

The communicative purpose of a genre, further, may evolve over time. It may change, it may expand or it may shrink (Swales
2004). Communicative purpose, further, can vary across cultures even when texts belong to the same genre category.

01: Write Types of Speech Acts.

Types of Speech Acts

There are various kinds of speech acts, yet the following, classified by John Searle,
have received particular attention:

Representatives

Commit a speaker to the truth of an expressed proposition.

Paradigm cases: asserting, stating, concluding, boasting, describing, suggesting.

      I am a great singer.
      Bill was an accountant.

Commissive

Commit a speaker to some future action.

Paradigm cases: promising, pledging, threatening, vowing, offering.

      I am going to leave you.
      I'll call you tonight.

Directives

Are used by a speaker who attempts to get the addressee to carry out an action.

Paradigm cases: requesting, advising, commanding, challenging, inviting, daring, and
entreating.

      You'd better tidy up that mess.
      Sit down.

Declarations

Affect an immediate change of affairs.

Paradigm cases: declaring, baptizing, resigning, firing from employment, hiring,
arresting.

      We find the defendant guilty.
      I resign.

Expressive

Express some sort of psychological state.

Paradigm cases: greeting, thanking, apologizing, complaining, congratulating.

      This beer is disgusting.
      I'm sorry to hear that.

02: What is Exchange Context?

An exchange is a sequence of discourse moves by at least two speakers that forms a
topical (or sub topical unit). A minimal exchange comprises an initiating move plus a
contribution by another speaker. There are two classes of exchanges; boundary
exchanges and teaching exchanges (Sinclair and Coulthard, 1992, pg.25). Boundary
exchanges contain two moves, framing and focusing moves. The only three principals
of teaching exchanges described by Sinclair and Coulthard are informing, directing,
and eliciting exchanges.

03: What is Eliciting Exchange?

The most common exchange in the classroom is an eliciting exchange (Willis, 1992,
pg.113). These exchanges begin with the teacher asking a question (usually one they
already know the answer to). An answer is then given by the student, and finally a follow-
up evaluation by the teacher. (Hellermann, 2003, pg.80). Here is an example from the
study done by Sinclair and Coulthard.

04: Differentiate between language ideologies and attitudes.

Language ideologies and language attitudes are conceptual tools used to understand
speakers' feelings and ideas about languages and linguistic forms. Both concepts
recognize the importance of linguistic subjectivity in understanding language change,
identity, and socioeconomic context. They share similarities in focusing on speakers'
feelings and beliefs about language structure and use. However, they differ in their
historical development, methodological approaches, and fields of concern.

Language attitudes typically involve quantitative measurement of speakers' reactions,
while language ideologies employ qualitative methods like ethnography, conversational
analysis, and discourse analysis. Language ideologies emphasize how speakers' beliefs

and feelings are shaped by their social experiences and political economic systems, and
how their awareness of language forms and functions is crucial.

Despite these differences, both concepts aim to understand speakers' perspectives on
language and its role in shaping identity and society. By recognizing the complementary
strengths of both approaches, researchers can gain a more comprehensive
understanding of language and its complex role in human communication.

05: what is Illocutionary act?

It is performed as an act of saying something or as an act of opposed to saying
something. The illocutionary utterance has a certain force of it. It well well-versed with
certain tones, attitudes, feelings, or emotions. There will be an intention of the speaker or
others in illocutionary utterance. It is often used as a tone of warning in day today life.

06: what is Spoken discourse?

Language’s use in face-to-face interactions such as conversations, meetings, and
discussions. Spoken discourse refers to the study and analysis of spoken language and
communication in real-time contexts. It encompasses various forms of verbal interactions,
such as conversations, dialogues, interviews, and speeches.

07: What is Discourse community?

A group of people who share a common language, values, and practices, often with a
shared goal or interest, and who use language to construct and maintain their identity and
relationships.

08: What is Conversation Analysis?

A methodology for studying social interactions, particularly conversations, to understand
how people use language to create social order and meaning. Conversation analysis (CA)
is an approach to the study of social interaction that emerged in the 1960s. Conversation
analysis works with recordings of spoken data and carries out careful and fine-grained
analyses of this data. Conversation analysis is an approach to the analysis of spoken
discourse that looks at the way in which people manage their everyday conversational
interactions. It examines how spoken discourse is organized and develops as speakers
carry out these interactions.

eng523-notes-for-mids-by-maha-malik-1-pd:
Adjacency pairs
An adjacency pair is a unit of conversation that contains an exchange of one turn each by two
speakers. The turns are functionally related to each other in such a fashion that the first turn
requires a certain type or range of types of second turn.
Big “C” Conversations (Tools of Inquiry)
“Conversations” (with a capital “C”) are debates in society or within specific social groups (over
focused issues like smoking, abortion, or school reform) that large numbers of people recognize,
both in terms of what “sides” there are to take in such debates and what sorts of people tend to be
on each side.
Collocational Patterns
Any pattern of words or grammatical structures (types of words and phrases and clauses) that
“hang together” to betoken a particular social language (and the identity associated with it) in the
way in which sun hat, swimsuit, sunscreen, a towel, and flip-flops “hang together” to betoken a
“sunbather.”
Conversational Analysis
A detailed form of discourse analysis that sees conversation as the basic human communicational
form and seeks to explicate how people produce and reproduce social order through talk and
orientation to talk and each other in social interaction. The approach is almost always just spelled
as “CA” and is a branch of sociology (one that gives up building grand sociological theories in
favor of describing the order people actually create and how they create and sustain that order).
Manny Schegloff at the University of California at Los Angeles is the best living practitioner of
CA.
Critical Discourse Analysis
Any form of discourse analysis that seeks to engage with politics (see the Glossary entry for
“politics”). Critical discourse analysis deals with whose “interests” are represented, helped, or
harmed as people speak and write. When “critical discourse analysis” is spelled as “CDA” it often
refers to the work of Norman Fairclough and his associates.
Eliciting Exchange
The most common exchange in the classroom is an eliciting exchange (Willis, 1992, pg.113).
These exchanges begin with the teacher asking a question (usually one they already know the
answer to).
Identity

A word used for lots of different things. What I mean by it in this book is this: Different ways of
being in the world at different times and places for different purposes; for example, ways of being
a “good student,” an “avid bird watcher,” a “mainstream politician,” a “tough cop,” a video-game
“gamer,” a “Native American,” and so on and so forth through a nearly endless list. I do not mean
your core sense of self, who you take yourself “essentially” to be, though that is an important
notion as well. I often use the term “socially situated identity” or “social identity” instead of just
the word “identity” to make clear I am talking about how we recognize and act out different social
roles or different social positions in society.
language Function
A language function refers to what students do with language as they engage with content and
interact with others.
Minimal Responses
Responses such as mmmm and yeah are known as minimal responses.
Semiotics
A term for the study of sign systems.
Sign
Any word or symbol (which could be an image or object) that has meaning (stands for something
else thanks to a given concept, interpretation, and convention which relates to the sign and the
thing it stands for).
Textual Pattern
A level of interpretation which we are involved in as we process texts is that of recognizing textual
pattern.
Utterance-Token Meaning
It refers to “situated meaning”.

1. Discursive psychology is a/an _______ that addresses psychological matters in terms of how they figure in discourse in conversations.
   Options:
   a) term
   b) technique
   c) method
   d) approach
   Correct answer: d) approach

2. The ________ research involves work in political science and to some degree in cultural studies.
   Options:
   a) quantitative
   b) non-linguistic
   c) sociolinguistic
   d) qualitative
   Correct answer: d) qualitative

3. The term _______ refers to statements or claims made about God or gods.
   Options:
   a) philosophy
   b) societal norms
   c) religious language
   d) cultural system
   Correct answer: c) religious language

4. Conversational experience and social context of language development is mediated by cognitive structures is known as _____________ approach.
   Options:
   a) structuralist
   b) sociocognitive
   c) noncognitive
   d) cognitive
   Correct answer: b) sociocognitive

5. Who argues that CDA should not be seen as a method but as a form of critically driven theory and practice?
   Options:
   a) Wodak and Meyer
   b) Wilson Smith
   c) Lakoff and Johnson
   d) Van Dijk
   Correct answer: a) Wodak and Meyer

6. What are the major units of analysis known as in a conversation?
   Options:
   a) Adjoining unit
   b) Adjacency unit
   c) Adjoining pair
   d) Adjacency pair

   Options:

   b) environmental sciences
   c) natural sciences

   Correct answer: a) social sciences

    a) applied linguistics
    b) psycholinguistics
    c) none of the given options
    d) applied psychology

Introduction to Discourse Analysis:
Discourse analysis is the study of language in use, focusing on how people
communicate and construct meaning through spoken or written texts. It examines
not only individual sentences but also the broader context, social interactions, and
cultural norms that shape communication. Discourse analysts explore various
aspects, including language patterns, power dynamics, and the impact of context
on meaning.
   Two Strands of Discourse Analysis:
There are two main strands within discourse analysis:
      o Micro-level analysis: This examines the structure of individual
          utterances, such as sentences or phrases. Researchers analyze linguistic
          features, syntax, and semantics to understand how meaning is
          conveyed.
      o Macro-level analysis: This zooms out to consider larger patterns, such
          as entire conversations, narratives, or discourses. It looks at social
          contexts, power relations, and cultural norms that influence
          communication.
   Discourse Markers and Conversation:
   Discourse markers are words or phrases that help organize and manage
   conversations. They signal transitions, emphasize points, or express attitudes.
   Examples include "so," "right," "okay," and "anyway." These markers play a
   crucial role in maintaining smooth communication.
   Discourse and Sociolinguistics:
   Sociolinguistics investigates how language varies across different social
   groups, regions, and contexts. It explores questions like why people speak

  differently based on their background, identity, and social status.
  Sociolinguists analyze language use in real-world situations, considering both
  individual and societal factors.
  Discourse and Speech Acts:
  Speech acts refer to utterances that not only convey information but also
  perform actions. When someone says, "I would like the kimchi; could you
  please pass it to me?" they express a desire (locutionary act) and make a
  request (illocutionary act). Speech acts highlight the pragmatic functions of
  language beyond literal meaning.
  Pragmatics and the Acquisition of Discourse:
  Pragmatics explores how context influences language use. It includes
  understanding implicatures, indirect speech, and politeness. When children
  acquire language, they learn not only grammar but also pragmatic rules for
  effective communication.
  Discourse: Gender, Racism, and Religion:
  Discourse analysis sheds light on how language reflects and perpetuates social
  issues. Researchers examine gendered language, racist discourse, and
  religious narratives. By analyzing texts, they uncover hidden biases and power
  dynamics..
